style: Read as a calm, intelligent documentary narrator, but brisk and urgent. Short sentences, clear pauses, no theatrics.

shorts.text:
Google pays Apple about twenty billion dollars.

In one year. For one setting.

Not a product. A default.

Here's what nobody checks. The search engine on your phone? You didn't choose it. Almost nobody does.

And that's the whole business. Whoever is the default gets the searches. Every search carries an ad.

Twenty twenty-two. About twenty billion dollars. For a setting nobody changes.

Google pays Apple about twenty billion dollars.

Google pays Apple thirty-six percent.

Of the search ad money from Safari.

That number wasn't supposed to leave the courtroom. An economist testifying for Google said it out loud. A Google lawyer reportedly winced.

Picture a toll booth. The cars are your searches. Every time a car passes, Google pays the toll. Not a fixed fee. A share.

So why would Apple ever build its own search engine?

It doesn't have to. It just collects.

Google pays Apple thirty-six percent.

A federal judge ruled that Google illegally kept a monopoly in search.

August twenty twenty-four.

A year later, the judge decided the punishment. And did not ban the payments.

Banned: exclusive deals. Allowed: the check.

Google can still pay Apple to be the default.

The monopoly was illegal. The payments are legal. Both are true.

Today, both sides are appealing.

The monopoly was illegal. The payments are legal.

One thing to do this week.

Open your phone. Go to your browser's settings. Find the search engine. Look at what it says.

You don't have to change it. But look.

Who chose it for you?

Behind that single line, in twenty twenty-two, was about twenty billion dollars.

One thing, this week. Look.
